name: PT Indo Tambangraya Megah Tbk

frontmatter.title: Indo Tambangraya Megah: a net-cash, high-CV Kalimantan producer whose dividend no longer covers the tape premium
frontmatter.summary: ITM sells high-CV Kalimantan coal at a fixed-price-driven discount to the Newcastle marker, runs net cash and pays a variable dividend. This revision answers the round-two challenges: the FY2026E cost base is re-based to the six-month run-rate on the guided strip, the buyback is computed rather than assumed away, and an onerous Indominco renewal is now charged. The rating stays HOLD and the target sits below the tape.
thesis: The current year's realised price is measured on the six-month actual, not read off a stable-ratio assumption: two-thirds of the sales book is fixed-price, so a rising marker is not passed through at the prior-year ratio [S2, F26].

Volume is the company's own plan, not our call: the current-year line sits inside the published indicative sales range, is held near the top of it through the near term and then eases onto a flat line, because the stated reserve base supports well over a decade at that rate and nothing in the mine plan sources a fade [S2, S3].

The balance sheet is the hinge: net cash, a small debt line and a newly sized buyback programme mean the dividend and the capital return, not the finite-life DCF, are what the market is capitalising [S0, S7].

Costs follow the mine plan rather than the prior-year blend: the strip ratio is held at the six-month run-rate and the purchased-coal book is re-based to the gap between the sales target and the production target [S2, S3].

The scenarios mirror on the benchmark and the domestic take, with the royalty charged in the bear; the one-stop export channel carries no disclosed fee or realised-price effect, so it is a monitored transition rather than a priced shock. The bear sizes its volume clip to the Indominco concession and the bull cannot mirror it upward because the work-plan quota caps output [S2, S6].

catalysts.event: Third-quarter FY2026 production and sales release; check sales against the indicative range, the realised price against the six-month actual and the strip sequence
FY2027 RKAB approval from ESDM; the quota sets next year's volume line
Coal exports must clear through state exporter PT DSI from 1 January; watch whether the Eksportir Terdaftar transition and customs clearance keep tonnes moving
Buyback programme closes on 4 February 2027: check the shares actually repurchased, the cash used and the residual net-cash position
Annual general meeting: final dividend declaration and any renewal of the buyback authority, the current programme having run to February 2027
Indominco Mandiri (CCOW Gen I) concession expiry; watch the extension or conversion route

blocks.text: **What changed (5 November 2026).** ITMG has disclosed a buyback of up to IDR2.31tn, running from 5 November 2026 to 4 February 2027 and funded from internal cash, with prior treasury shares and the new purchases together capped at 20.0% of paid-up capital [S7, F41, F44]. The company's proforma puts the post-programme count at 1,026m shares and shows a mechanical EPS and ROE uplift [S7, F43]. We now compute it rather than assume it away: the cash spent is a negative item in the valuation bridge and the proforma count is carried in the share-change input, so the per-share effect is negative because the purchase price is above our through-cycle value, and the transfer runs from continuing holders to sellers [S7, F43, F45]. The house market and peer-multiple refresh in the same window re-based the cross-check legs, so the target is Rp20,483, down from the prior published target, and the rating stays HOLD. The remainder of the 31 October revision is carried forward: the current-year realised price measured on the six-month actual with the fixed-price book rolling off, the strip held at the run-rate, the purchased-coal book rebuilt against the sales and production targets, discretionary expansion capex excluded symmetrically, the one-stop export rule as a monitored transition risk rather than a priced shock, and the IFRS 16 lease treatment as an operating cost rather than a second deduction from equity [S2, S3, S6].

We keep PT Indo Tambangraya Megah Tbk at **HOLD** with a twelve-month target of **Rp20,483** against a last price of Rp24,350: a total return of **-6.0%** on our probability-weighted scenarios, with the dividend no longer enough to carry the equity past the tape. The company is the Indonesian thermal-coal arm of the Banpu group: four CCoW concessions in East and Central Kalimantan plus a clutch of IUPs, producing a high-calorific-value product, with the Imm and Tcm coals well up the grade range [S2], sold to China, Japan, India and the domestic power market from a net-cash balance sheet [S3].

Our through-cycle NAV — a full-life DCF carried to reserve depletion with no terminal value, not a cut at the maximum-cumulative-PV year — is **Rp15,791**, below the tape, because the coal deck's long-run Newcastle marker mean-reverts below spot and we do not capitalise the war premium. The life runs to the year the 382 Mt reserve is exhausted on the modelled sales rate; free cash flow turns negative in the late reserve years at deck prices, but the working-capital release as the reserve runs out more than offsets them, so the tail adds under one per cent to the value rather than subtracting from it and we carry it [S0]. The dividend method is what lifts the blended value above it: on the modelled payout the shares support a dividend-capacity yield capitalised at **Rp20,937** [S0], the anchor the market has paid for this name, though no longer enough to reach the price. Both cross-checks sit above the DCF — EV/EBITDA at Rp31,200 (97.6% above) and the dividend method at Rp20,937 (32.6% above) — so the blended value sits between the finite-life value and the market's multiple, below the tape.

The variant view: the tape implies the Newcastle benchmark holds near **US$130/t** through the horizon, a factor of 1.1 on the FY2027E deck marker [S0], which we think is too generous on price and not too harsh on volume. Three things move the value: the benchmark, the RKAB quota that sets the volume line, and the domestic take under the standing cap [S2, S3].

PT Indo Tambangraya Megah Tbk is an Indonesian thermal-coal producer, listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange since 2007 and now a subsidiary of Banpu Minerals (Singapore) Pte. Ltd., which holds 65.1% of the shares indirectly through Banpu Public Company Limited, with the balance in public hands and a small treasury position [S3, S2]. It reports in US dollars, sells in US dollars, and employs 1,609.0 people [S0]. The group's own structure slide shows the controlling chain — Banpu at roughly two thirds, the public at roughly a third, and a small treasury-share position [S2].

The business is a single commodity with a diversified mine portfolio: four CCoW concessions — Indominco Mandiri (CCOW Gen I, East Kalimantan), Trubaindo (Gen II), Bharinto Ekatama (Gen III) and Jorong Barutama Greston (Gen II, South Kalimantan) — plus four IUPs (Graha Panca Karsa, Tepian Indah Sukses, Nusa Persada Resources, Kitadin) [S3]. The product mix is skewed to the higher grades — Imm, Tcm and Bek — while Jbg, Gpk and Npr sit lower [S2]. That grade mix is what makes the realised price key off the Newcastle and HBA markers rather than the low-grade ICI indices [S2].

Alongside the coal book the group runs adjacent businesses that are small against it: coal trading through an energy-commodities subsidiary, mining contractor and port services, a barge port serving the Melak cluster, and a rooftop-solar arm [S2, S3], plus a mineral-sector vehicle stood up in October 2026 [S4]. None is material to value, and we no longer charge their expansion spend while crediting no return: no archived filing discloses segment revenue, a project value or a separable sunk capex for these assets, and the company reports no material capital commitments and no realised capital-goods investment for the year [S2, S3, S4]. We therefore exclude the discretionary capex from the coal cash flow and carry the optionality at nil, symmetrically, rather than at an invented number [S3].

The competitive position is a mid-sized, high-grade, low-cost Indonesian producer: a price-taker on the marker whose unit cost sits inside the band the peer COAL names book, not a claimed quartile of a global curve we cannot source [S3]. Its reserve base was 382 Mt of JORC reserves at the end of 2025 [S3, F11]; on the production plan of 22.9 Mt that is a reserve life of roughly seventeen years. The DCF itself runs that life to depletion with no terminal value: the late-life years are cash-negative at deck prices, but the working-capital release as the reserve runs out keeps the tail modestly value-additive, which is why the model carries the full life rather than cutting the DCF at the maximum-cumulative-PV year [S0]. The company announced a buyback of up to IDR2.31tn on 4 November 2026, running three months [S7, F41]; it is a capital-return lever that does not enter the valuation when the shares trade above our through-cycle value. The nearest expiry is the Indominco concession in March 2028, which is also the largest single production unit [S2].

Thermal coal is a cyclical, dollar-priced, policy-shaped commodity, and the deck we work from frames it that way: the Newcastle 6,000 kcal/kg marker is the price series, the DMO cap is the administered ceiling on domestic power tonnes, and the coal deck's long-run view is that the marginal Indonesian tonne clears in a band around its long-run marker once the war premium fades [S0]. Our industry read is that supply discipline, not demand growth, is what has held the price up: the company's own market commentary names Indonesian RKAB uncertainty and higher domestic-market obligations as the supply constraint, alongside logistics disruption in South Africa and Colombia and the war-driven diesel shortage in Russia, with Chinese domestic output and Indian import substitution the two demand-side dampeners [S2].

Regulation is the swing factor. Coal sits under the RKAB annual work-plan approval, which sets each producer's permitted volume, and under the domestic market obligation that reserves a share of output for the national power market at the administered cap [S2, S3]. The royalty regime depends on the licence: the CCoW mines pay a contract-specific rate and the IUP mines the lower schedule, and the royalty the group actually booked was 220 USD m on net revenue of US$1,881.1m in the last year, below the contract headline [S3]. We set the licence to the work-agreement regime and the royalty to the booked effective rate, and justify both in the model.

The newest layer is the export channel. Exports of strategic resources must be handled by the state export company PT Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia from 1 January 2027, under PP No. 24/2026 and Permendag No. 15/2026 [S6]. The coal Eksportir Terdaftar licence is valid only to 31 December 2026; after that the state exporter is the only permitted channel, and producers must report export documents and contracts to it through an integrated system [S6]. APBI warns that treating it as a formality could leave coal unable to be exported on 1 January 2027 [S6]. The export base is 19.2 Mt of the 24.7 Mt sold in the last year [S3, F21]. The exposure is process rather than price — nothing reported sets a fee or a different realised price — so neither scenario shocks it, and it stays a shipment-timing risk and a monitoring item [S6].

The moat is grade and cost position rather than scale: a high-CV product carried at a unit cost inside the peer band is what survives a trough, and ITM's strip ratio and unit cost sit inside that band rather than above it [S3]. Its pricing power is nil on the marker and real on the mix — but the mix cuts both ways, and the previous edition overstated the pass-through: because 67.0% of current-year sales are fixed-price and only a quarter indexed, a move in the marker reaches the realised price with a lag, and the ratio falls when the marker rises [S2, F26]. That is what the six-month print shows, and why we measure the ratio on the latest actual. On the five forces, supplier power is moderate (contract mining and fuel, with diesel the live cost pressure), buyer power is high, substitutes are real but slow — with gas-to-coal switching in Japan, Korea and Taiwan holding thermal demand firm [S2] — new entrants are gated by permits, capital and the RKAB, and rivalry is disciplined by the same regime.

The five-year record is a classic coal cycle. Revenue ran at US$3,636.2m in the peak year, fell to US$2,374.3m and US$2,304.5m, and reached US$1,881.1m in the last actual year [S0, S3]. The compression is entirely price: volumes were steady at 24.0 and 24.7 of sales tonnage in the last two years [S3], while the realised price fell from 95.7 to 76.0 [S5]. Gross margin narrowed with it, and net profit to parent fell to US$190.9m [S0].

Our forecast rebuilds the same way: revenue is volume times a capped realised price, with volume the company's own current-year range held flat [S2], and the realised price the deck's Newcastle marker times a ratio measured on the six-month actual for the current year and fitted on the last two completed years thereafter, because the fixed book rolls off [S5, S2]. That gives first-forecast-year revenue of US$2,203.5m at a realised price of 81.0, the six-month actual held into the full year and above the 76.0 of last year, and an EBITDA of US$321.0m that reproduces the last actual year on more tonnes, with the deeper strip and the larger purchased-coal book absorbing the price gain [S0, S2 p.21].

Costs are where caution usually creeps in, and we have kept it out. Cash cost per tonne is the physical strip ratio times the mining cost per cubic metre, backed out of the LK's cost-of-revenue note, plus a residual for hauling, barging, processing and the purchased-coal book [S3]. The strip is held at the six-month run-rate because the company's quarterly disclosure has the pits deepening and the ratio guided higher at the two largest mines [S2]. The purchased book is rebuilt, not inherited: mining costs of 653.3 US$m and coal purchases of 256.3 US$m sit in the LK note [S3], and the gap between the sales target and the production target implies more purchased tonnes than the prior-year mix [S2]. Royalty is the booked effective rate, not the contract headline [S3], and SG&A is held at the last actual's share of revenue because the step-up reads as structural [S3]. Tax is the data pack's three-year average effective rate of 26.2%, held flat [S0]: it sits below the last actual year's effective charge, which we read as a single-year outcome rather than the forward rate, and that is the one unhedged optimistic departure in the forecast, disclosed here rather than smoothed away and not large enough to move the rating on its own.

We restate depreciation rather than model around it: the pack's prior-year figure is a stub because the cash-flow statement uses the direct method, so we take the LK's own charge for the last two years and let the engine rebuild history [S3]. The line we carry is the property, plant and equipment depreciation charged to cost of revenue; right-of-use depreciation is treated as an operating cost and sits in the selling and G&A lines the unit-cost build reconciles to [S3]. That is why our last-year EBITDA (operating income plus that PPE charge) sits below the company's presented EBITDA of 343 USD m: the company adds back total D&A, of which right-of-use depreciation is 36.9 USD m [S5 p.23, S3]. The gap is a definitional lease treatment, not a cost we have missed, and the 35.5 USD m of cash lease payments in the LK's cash-flow statement bears it out [S3]. We do not add the right-of-use charge back a second time, and we do not deduct the lease liability from equity.

The bridge uses the company's own 30 June 2026 balance sheet: cash of 738 USD m against borrowings of 18.0 USD m, a net-cash position [S2]. The data pack's larger cash and debt lines are not used. Its debt line is total debt including lease liabilities, and the lease component is a derived residual — the pack's total-debt line less the company's borrowings — not a figure the company discloses line-by-line at the interim date. The last disclosed lease liability was 40.4 USD m current plus 9.8 USD m non-current at 31 December 2025 [S3 p.142]; the increase to the interim date is an inference from the new vessel, port and mine leases signed since, not a filing figure, and the valuation does not rest on it. The pack's cash line does not tie to the interim disclosure either, so the two balance sheets are reconciled by adopting the company's [S2, S3 p.142]. Capex is sustaining spend per tonne, held flat in nominal terms; the LK's total reconciles as 79.0 USD m of property, plant and equipment purchases plus 40.7 USD m of deferred exploration and development (the deferred-stripping build) [S3], and the six-month run-rate is well below the prior-year average [S2]. Discretionary expansion spend is excluded for the business-section reason [S3, S2, S4]. Working capital is thin and held at the historical ratio, and no new borrowing is assumed [S0, S2].

Earnings quality. ITM is clean. On the card's accruals test, net profit less operating cash flow over average total assets is negative — operating cash flow of 285.5 US$m exceeded net profit of US$194.7m in the last year, and the prior year shows the same sign [S0, S3] — so earnings are cash-backed and receivables fell on lower prices [S0]. There is no special-notation or special-board flag; the shares trade in the main market and the LK is audited and unqualified [S3]. Related-party gravity is low and quantified: coal sales to related parties were under 1.0% of net revenue and related-party marketing about a tenth of selling expenses, disclosed and arm's length [S3, F30]. The controlling holder has roughly two thirds; a buyback of up to IDR2.31tn running to February 2027 was disclosed on 4 November 2026 [S7, F41]. The arithmetic is now shown rather than assumed. The programme spends up to IDR2.31tn of cash, roughly a fifth of the net-cash balance, and the company's proforma retires enough shares to cut the count to 1,026m, a reduction of about eight per cent [S7, F43]. Both legs are in the model: the cash leaves the valuation bridge as a negative item and the smaller count is carried in the share-change input, so the dividend per share rises on the reduced base while the equity value falls by the cash spent. Because the programme is executed above our through-cycle value, the net effect on value per share is negative: the DCF leg falls and the dividend leg rises, leaving the blend lower than it would be without the programme. The cap of 20.0% of paid-up capital also includes the existing treasury position [S2], so the headroom for new purchases is smaller than the headline. There is no rights-issue or discounted-placement pattern [S3, S2]. One optics-class flag: the variable dividend is a board decision, carried at the LK's latest rate [S0, S3].

Indonesian thermal coal producers have historically been valued less on the life of their reserves than on the cash they return, because the reserve life is long relative to the policy horizon and the cash-return decision is annual.

We value ITM on the house method for commodity producers: a through-cycle discounted cash flow over the mine's economic life as the primary method, an EV/EBITDA cross-check and a dividend-capacity cross-check, weighted **60.0%**, **25.0%** and **15.0%** [S0]. The fit is that the value is a finite, price-taking cash-flow stream: a cyclical producer should never be valued on spot earnings, and the primary DCF runs the mine's finite life at the deck's through-cycle prices with no terminal value, carried to reserve depletion rather than cut at the maximum-cumulative-PV year [S0].

The cost of capital is built from the house inputs: a risk-free rate of 4.9%, a mature-market premium of 4.2%, a country premium of 2.5%, and an unlevered beta of 0.80 lifting to 0.81 levered at the statutory tax rate of 22.0% [S0]. That gives a cost of equity of **10.3%** and a WACC of **10.2%** [S0]. We carry no governance premium: related-party flows are small and there is no controlling-stake pledge on the register [S3].

The primary method gives **Rp15,791** per share, below the tape, and the reason is the deck, not the company: the long-run marker is flat in real terms and well below spot, the war premium is a cycle position, and the realised price is a fraction of the marker [S0]. The DCF runs on sales tonnes, so the purchased book draws down the reserve statement — a shortcut that shortens the modelled life by a couple of years against the production plan and biases the NAV down a little, at the same time as the purchased margin it earns is credited. The engine runs the full life to depletion with no terminal value. Free cash flow is thin through FY2033E and negative from FY2034E to FY2039E at deck prices as the strip bites and the reserve runs down, but the working-capital release in the final years more than offsets those negative years, so the tail adds under one per cent to the NAV and the DCF is carried to depletion rather than truncated. Net of the small debt line, the enterprise value is 314.3 [S0].

The cross-checks diverge, and the divergence is the point. EV/EBITDA gives **Rp31,200**, 97.6% above the primary, because the peer multiple blends names trading on a war-premium cash flow [S0]. The dividend method gives **Rp20,937**, 32.6% above, because it capitalises last year's cash return rather than the finite-life value [S0]. We state the multiple: the leg capitalises the modelled dividend at **11.5%**, against a forward yield on our own modelled payout of 9.9% [S0]. That multiple is the house blend of the peer median and ITM's own trailing-yield average, and the own-history leg rests on three observations that include the 2022-23 supercycle, so it is not a through-cycle anchor. At the forward yield the leg would be materially higher, which is why we call the dividend leg the most generous of the three rather than a value we would defend. We carry both at their house weights: the market is paying for the cash return, and the finite-life value is the floor beneath it. The EV/EBITDA leg is a re-rating to a war-premium peer multiple rather than a through-cycle value: the multiple the engine uses blends the peer median with ITM's own trailing average across the four years the pack carries, and on the own-history half of that blend alone the leg would sit only around a third above the DCF, so the range, not the blended number, is the cross-check [S0]. The buyback is now in the arithmetic, on both legs. Its cash cost enters `valuation.bridge` as a negative item and the proforma count reduction enters the share-change input, so the DCF leg is struck on the smaller post-programme share count and net of the cash spent, while the dividend leg earns the higher per-share payout on the same reduced count [S7, F41, F43, F45]. The net effect is negative because the purchase price is above our through-cycle value: the shares retired cost more than they are worth, and the transfer runs from continuing holders to sellers. The programme is shown in the financial analysis and governance sections as well.

What the price implies: run the DCF backwards and the tape requires the Newcastle benchmark near **US$130/t**, a factor of 1.1 on the FY2027E deck marker [S0]. That embeds the war premium persisting, a low-yield dividend capitalisation and no policy surprise. We do not think the premium persists on the current-year economics, and our target sits below the price because the dividend and the probability-weighted near-term cash return no longer cover the gap between the tape and the finite-life value.

The downside risks. **Regulatory** (medium likelihood, high impact): the RKAB cycle sets the volume line and the domestic obligation diverts tonnes to the capped power market [S2]. **Concession** (medium, high): the Indominco CCoW expires in March 2028 and is the largest single production unit with the thinnest reserve base, so an onerous extension hits volume and royalty [S2]. **Export channel** (medium, medium): from 1 January 2027 coal may be exported only through PT DSI, and APBI warns an unprepared transition could stall shipments [S6]; no source attaches a fee or a realised-price effect to it, so neither scenario prices it and it is carried as a shipment-timing risk rather than a shock. **Macro** (medium, high): the complex carries a war premium and the deck sees the long-run marker well below spot, so mean reversion is the base case [S0]. **FX** (low, medium): dollar revenue against a partly rupiah cost base [S3]. **Operational** (medium, medium): the mine plan raises the strip ratio as pits deepen [S2]. **Governance and liquidity** (low, low): related-party flows are small, there is no pledge, and the shares are liquid [S3, S0]. **Capital allocation** (medium, medium): the buyback programme of up to IDR2.31tn runs from 5 November 2026 to 4 February 2027 and is funded from internal cash [S7, F41]; the shares trade above our through-cycle value, so execution transfers value between holders rather than creating it.

Our scenarios are mirrored on the benchmark and the capped domestic share, and we have not stacked the bear. The price shocks are specified as a symmetric full-cycle move from FY2027, the house default, but because the engine multiplies the whole forecast, each leg uses the present-value-equivalent uniform multiplier: the elapsed current year, three-quarters actual and at the reviewed spot, is not shocked, and the tail carries the full move. The bear raises the domestic take, adds to the booked royalty, and sizes the volume clip to the Indominco concession: the mine is 7.1 Mt of the 22.9 Mt current-year production plan [S2], holds 31.0 Mt of reserves and its CCoW expires in March 2028 [S2], so a failed extension removes about three-tenths of mined volume. Because the engine shocks the whole forecast, the volume clip is likewise a present-value equivalent. The bull mirrors the benchmark and the domestic take, and runs volume at the top of the company's own guided sales range rather than above it; it cannot mirror the bear's volume cut upward because the work-plan quota and the guidance cap output [S2, F15], so it earns its return from price rather than from invented volume. Neither leg shocks the required return. The bear does now charge the royalty: an onerous Indominco renewal that lifts the booked rate toward the contract headline is a step of under two percentage points on the royalty rate, and it is unmirrored in the bull because no sourced mechanism lets the booked rate fall [S3].

On those shocks the bear is **Rp16,240**, the bull **Rp26,836** and the base **Rp20,102**, at probabilities of 0.25, 0.55 and 0.20 [S0]. The bull carries a smaller weight than the bear because its volume upside is capped by the company's own guidance while the bear's Indominco mechanism is a live concession expiry; the price legs themselves are mirrored, and the macro desk is neutral on thermal coal with the deck flagging spot as a war-premium carry, not a level [S0]. The base dominates because the most probable path is the company's own plan at the deck's prices.

The rating is not presented as more robust than it is. The base value of **Rp20,102** is below the last price of Rp24,350, so the base price-only return is negative and the total return stays negative even after the dividend; only the bull clears the tape. With the bear weight doubled and the bull cut correspondingly the probability-weighted value would sit further below the last price, which is why we do not underwrite the target on the bull's convexity. The HOLD is a valuation call: the dividend is no longer enough to cover the premium the tape pays over the value of the mine's finite life, and a lower entry would be needed to make the total return positive. The signposts that would change the view: an RKAB outcome below the indicative range; a domestic obligation above the current share; whether the export channel clears coal without a shipment gap in early 2027 [S6]; a sustained marker move either side of the deck path; the Indominco extension terms; and a buyback executed below our through-cycle value.

Ownership is straightforward. Banpu Minerals (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. holds 65.1% indirectly through Banpu Public Company Limited, with the public holding the balance and a small treasury position [S3, S2]. The register shows no pledged controlling stake and no margin-call structure [S3]. The audit is unqualified and the accounts carry the coal-specific royalty and stripping disclosures the sector needs [S3].

On related parties, coal sales to related parties were under 1.0% of net revenue and related-party marketing about a tenth of selling expenses, disclosed and arm's length [S3, F30]. We found no discounted placement, no serial rights issue and no auditor down-tier change. The buyback programme of up to IDR2.31tn disclosed on 4 November 2026 runs from 5 November 2026 to 4 February 2027, is capped at 20.0% of paid-up capital and is a capital-return decision we do not value because the shares trade above our through-cycle value [S7, F41, F44].

The dividend record is variable: the LK's payout-ratio disclosure shows the group distributing of the order of three-fifths of each year's profit with no formulaic floor [S0, S3], which we carry at the latest rate. On ESG, the group reports third-party ESG scores in its own disclosure but names neither the score nor a sector median we can verify, so we do not claim a relative position; what is disclosed is emissions work on biodiesel substitution and grid power and rehabilitation on post-mining forest return [S2]. A thermal-coal producer carries an unavoidable transition discount; what is controllable is capital discipline and reclamation, and both read as adequate [S2, S3].

The dated catalysts are the third-quarter operational release (sales against the indicative FY2026 range, the realised price against the six-month actual, the strip against guidance), the FY2027 RKAB approval that sets next year's volume, the 1 January 2027 switch to the state export channel which is the first live test of whether tonnes clear [S6], the annual general meeting that declares the final dividend and may consider renewing the buyback authority, and the Indominco expiry in the medium term [S2, S3].

Between updates we monitor the sector dashboard's KPIs: sales volume against the range; the realised price against the deck, re-checked every quarter; the strip ratio and unit cash cost against the mine plan; the booked royalty rate, the cleanest early signal of a regime change; EBITDA per tonne; reserves, which set the horizon; net debt, which stays negative; the payout ratio, the market's anchor; and, from January 2027, the export share cleared through the state exporter and any transition delay [S0, S3, S6]. The royalty rate and the reserve statement matter most, because either would re-price the model or change how long it runs. The fixed-price book means the realisation ratio moves with the direction of the marker, so a shift of more than a few points is the single assumption most likely to be wrong in either direction.

bear.narrative: The war premium unwinds and overshoots: the bear takes the deck's Newcastle path down 20% from FY2027 - the house default and the mirror of the bull - a demand-led trough through the marginal-cost floor the coal deck itself names as the level at which marginal Indonesian supply clears. FY2026 is NOT shocked: the year is three-quarters elapsed at the reviewed spot, so the whole-forecast multiplier is set at 0.91, which at the model's price-path weights is the PV-equivalent of holding the elapsed year at the deck and applying 0.8 from FY2027 (about 55% of the price-path PV sits in FY2026). The volume shock is now sized to the Indominco Mandiri concession, not a generic clip: IMM is 7.1 Mt of the 22.9 Mt top of the FY26 production plan [S2, F27, F28], holds only 31 Mt of reserves [S2, F29] and its CCoW Gen I expires in March 2028 [S2], so a failed extension removes about three-tenths of mined volume; the engine applies shocks to the whole forecast, so the banked clip is the PV-equivalent loss across the horizon. The government also raises the share of tonnes diverted to the capped domestic power market. The one-stop export transition (PP No. 24/2026, state exporter PT DSI from January 2027 [S6]) is NOT shocked: it carries no disclosed fee or realised-price effect, so it stays a shipment-timing risk and a monitoring item rather than a priced driver, which also keeps the bear inside the four-shock limit. The renewal is now CHARGED, not just described (round-2 C4): an IMM extension on onerous terms - a conversion or extension that lifts the booked royalty toward the 13.5% CCoW headline [S3] - is carried as a 1.8pp add to the booked 11.7% rate, which is the step from the group's blended rate to the contract headline on the 7.1 Mt IMM block. That is the middle outcome the base case was missing, and it is applied in the bear rather than the base because the extension decision is binary at March 2028 and no source prices a specific extension fee. The lower benchmark with the LK-rate payout cuts the dividend mechanically, so the bear value and the dividend cut arrive together. No re-rating or required-return shock is taken.

bull.narrative: The mirror of the bear on the same four drivers: the war premium holds and Chinese mine-safety curbs plus Indonesian RKAB discipline keep seaborne supply tight into 2027, so the benchmark runs 20% above the deck's path from FY2027 and ITM's high-CV Kalimantan coals capture the premium in full; FY2026 is held at the reviewed spot rather than shocked (the whole-forecast multiplier of 1.09 is the PV-equivalent of the elapsed year at the deck plus 1.2 from FY2027, and puts the FY2026 marker at about the US$150.4 reviewed spot [S0]); the export-channel transition clears without a shipment gap, so it adds no shock; volumes run at the TOP of the company's own guided sales range (27.5 of a 27.2 Mt base), not above it, because no archived source quantifies Bunyut throughput or an NPR uplift; and the domestic-market take eases back as export economics improve. The volume asymmetry against the bear is deliberate and sourced: upside is capped by the RKAB and the company's own 26.9-27.5 Mt sales target [S2, F15], so a symmetric three-tenths uplift is not physically available and the bull earns its return from price. The probability weight is cut to reflect the smaller volume upside. The royalty rate and the required return are NOT shocked: no sourced mechanism lets the booked royalty rate fall, and a bull that assumes a re-rating would be a defect. The buyback programme is a capital-return lever only if executed below our through-cycle value; the shares trade above it, so no buyback credit is taken and the programme is not shocked in either leg [S7, F41].

12-month value vs volume and unit cost intensity

OPS.label: Cash cost + royalty per unit (price currency)

football.label: DCF to end of life (no terminal value)

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the company's own published target, not our guess: the 2Q26 analyst presentation puts FY26 indicative coal sales at 26.9-27.5 Mt [S2, F15] against FY2025 actual sales of 24.7 Mt [S3, F1] and 6M26 sales of 12.3 Mt [S2]. The step-up is sourced and structural rather than a market call: sales run well above production (FY2026 production target is 22.0-22.9 Mt against a 26.9-27.5 Mt sales target [S2]) because the group draws down ROM and stockpile inventory and resells purchased coal through its trading arm, so the FY2026 sales line is the company's, held near the midpoint. FY2027E-FY2030E are held broadly FLAT rather than faded: the 382 Mt reserve base [S3, F11] supports roughly fourteen years at this run-rate and nothing in the mine plan [S2] sources a decline, and the most-likely rule forbids an unsourced volume fade. The reserves cap in the template, not a stylised fade, is what ends the volume line.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: RE-BASED ON THE 6M26 ACTUAL, not on a lagged H1 ratio. FY2026E 0.614 is set so that the engine reproduces the company's own six-month realised price: at the deck's FY2026E Newcastle marker (US$137.0), 0.78 x 0.614 x 137.0 + 0.22 x 70.0 = US$81.0/t, which is exactly the 6M26 ASP [S2 p.21] (F16 is the 2Q26 print of US$82.7/t, not the six-month figure). The previous 0.655 was the raw H1 ratio (US$81.0 over the H1-2026 average of about US$128.9) applied to a full-year marker 6% above the H1 level, which implicitly required an H2 ASP step-up that the contract book does not support: 67% of FY26 sales are fixed-price and only 24% indexed [S2, F26], so only about a quarter of the book can respond to a rising marker within the year. Holding the current year at the six-month actual is the most-likely read, not a haircut: it is the last actual, and the fixed two-thirds is locked. FY2027E-FY2030E revert to 0.7167, the ratio fitted on the last two completed fiscal years (FY2025A ASP US$76.0/t [S5, F3] over the deck's US$108.4 = 0.701; FY2024A US$95.7/t [S5, F4] over US$136.1 = 0.703, lifted to 0.7167 for the 22% capped domestic share), because the fixed 2026 book rolls off and the two-actual level is the through-cycle anchor. ITM's realised price is structurally below the Newcastle 6,000 marker: the product is a blend of 5,600-6,200 kcal/kg GAR (IMM) and higher-CV TCM/BEK coals [S2, F17], a fifth of tonnes go to the domestic market at HBA/DMO-linked prices [S3, F12], and the method card has Indonesian coal key off HBA/ICI rather than Newcastle. The FY2025A calibration gate is answered in qc_justifications.calibration.ebitda: it re-prices history at the FY2026E ratio, a forecast-year measurement, not a mis-specified cost base.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: The company's own disclosed domestic share: 5.5 Mt of the 24.7 Mt sold in FY2025 went to the Indonesian domestic market [S3, F12], i.e. 22.3% of sales volume, and those tonnes settle at HBA/DMO-linked prices against the standing US$70/t power cap carried in the coal deck (d.coal.dmo_cap). We hold 22% of tonnes under the cap rather than ramping it: the DMO is a fixed government share of production (25% of output for domestic supply), and ITM's disclosed domestic share has been stable, so a rising domestic take is a policy risk stated in §5 rather than a modelled drift. Capped tonnes receive min(cap, realised price), which bites hardest in the bull case.

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Carried as the PHYSICAL overburden-to-coal ratio (bcm/t) on the AADI/GEMS/BUMI peer convention, so that strip_ratio x cost_per_bcm is the mining block per tonne and is directly comparable with the other COAL names. RE-BASED ON THE COMPANY'S OWN 3Q26 GUIDES after the round-2 challenge (C5). The 6M26 group average of 10.3x [S2, F18] is an H1 number and the company has already guided the pits deeper for the second half: IMM 14.0x on 1.9 Mt, TCM 17.6x on 0.8 Mt and BEK 7.7x on 2.3 Mt in 3Q26 [S2 pp.17-18], which is 11.68x on a production-weighted basis across those three mines and about 10.9x once the remaining ~0.7 Mt at roughly 5x is added (0.7 x 5 = 3.5; (26.6 + 14.1 + 17.7 + 3.5) / 5.7 = 10.9x). FY2026E is therefore the volume-weighted blend of the two halves actually known: 12.3 Mt at the 6M26 actual 10.3x and the guided 14.9 Mt at 10.9x, i.e. (12.3 x 10.3 + 14.9 x 10.9) / 27.2 = 10.6x. FY2027E onward holds 10.9x, the guided 3Q26 group rate as the last guidance, and does not compound further: the reserve statement [S3, F11] gives no basis for a permanent climb, and the 6M26 print of 10.3x shows the deep 3Q26 IMM and TCM ratios are partly a pit-sequencing effect rather than a new permanently higher cost base. This replaces the 10.3/10.4x path, which charged none of the guided step and was the largest optimistic lever in the round-1 model.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: The overburden-removal and coal-getting cost per bank cubic metre. Backed out of the LK's own cost-of-revenue note: mining costs of US$653.3m on 24.7 Mt sold [S3, F1] is US$26.45/t, and at the FY2025A strip ratio of 9.4x [S3, F7] that is US$2.81/bcm — inside the US$2.6-8.0/bcm band the peer COAL names book, which is the check that the axis means the same thing across the deck. It escalates with the USD deck thereafter rather than falling in real terms, because the company names rising diesel and contract-mining rates as the live cost pressure (the presentation shows fuel at US$0.99/litre in 6M26 against US$0.78 a year earlier [S2]) and nothing in the filings sources a real decline.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Residual per-tonne cash cost ex-royalty and ex-D&A. RECALIBRATED TO THE 6M26 ACTUAL after the round-2 challenge (C1): the round-1 US$20.7/t was a bottom-up build off the FY2025 cost note and left the FY2026E line below the run-rate the company has already printed. The reconstruction: 6M26 revenue of US$1,000m at an US$81.0 ASP on 12.3 Mt gave a company-basis EBITDA of US$181.2m [S2 p.25, p.21]; on the model's lease basis (right-of-use and other D&A in the cost lines, not added back) that is about US$156m, or US$12.7/t. In the second half the guided 10.9x strip (vs 10.3x in H1) adds about US$1.7/t of cost, so H2 runs near US$11.0/t on the same ASP, giving a full-year line of US$156m + 14.9 Mt x US$11.0 = about US$320m on 27.2 Mt (US$11.8/t). At the modelled 10.6x strip and US$2.81/bcm the mining block contributes US$31.6/t, leaving US$18.8/t here. This is the residual that reconciles the model to the last actual, and it is consistent with the LK note from which the round-1 build started: the FY2025 cost of revenue of US$1,398.3m [S0] less royalty of US$220.0m [S3, F10] less depreciation of US$26.9m [S3, F8] over 24.7 Mt is US$46.6/t ex-royalty ex-D&A, of which mining was US$653.3m [S3, F24] and purchased coal US$256.3m [S3, F23]; the lower residual is the part of the FY2025 build (haul, barge, salaries, forestry, repairs, fuel) that the 6M26 actual shows running below the FY2025 average once the mining block is priced at the current strip. FY2026 sales of 27.2 Mt against a 22.0-22.9 Mt production target [S2, F28] implies about 4.75 Mt of purchased coal, which sits in this residual. SG&A is NOT here: ITM's selling and administrative expenses run at 11.5% of revenue and the engine carries them in opex_pct. Escalated gently with services and labour inflation thereafter.

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK notes, not the data pack. ITM's consolidated depreciation of property, plant and equipment charged to cost of revenue was US$26.86m in FY2025 and US$38.71m in FY2024 [S3, F8, F9]. The pack's FY2025A D&A of US$32.5m is in the right region but its FY2024A figure of US$1.3m is a stub, because the IDX cash-flow statement is presented on the direct method and carries no D&A add-back — which is exactly the restatement the method card asks for. THE RIGHT-OF-USE TREATMENT IS DELIBERATE AND IS NOT AN OMISSION: ROU depreciation was US$36.9m in FY2025 (US$32.5m of it in selling expenses [S3, F32]) and the ROU asset balance rose from US$3.0m to US$47.1m as new vessel, port and mine leases were capitalised [S3, F38]. We do NOT add that back here: the leases are treated as an operating cost, the cost lines the unit build reconciles to already carry the ROU depreciation, and the US$35.5m of cash lease payments [S3, F33] matches it. Adding ROU back to EBITDA/FCFF while also choosing to pay the lease cash out of the same cost base would double-count. This is why the model's FY2025A EBITDA (US$293.5m = operating income + PPE depreciation in cost of revenue) sits below the company's presented EBITDA of US$343.1m, which adds the total D&A of US$76.2m back [S5 p.23]: the difference is ROU depreciation plus the ~US$12m of other depreciation/amortisation that sits in the cost lines. Held at the FY2025A rate of US$1.09/t thereafter on the flat volume path.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Sustaining capital only. The FY2025 capex of US$119.7m on the data pack reconciles to the LK cash-flow statement as US$79.0m of property, plant and equipment purchases plus US$40.7m of deferred exploration and development (the deferred-stripping build) [S3, F36, F37], i.e. US$4.85/t total. Both legs are sustaining-grade spend tied to the mine: the deferred stripping is a direct function of the strip ratio, and the Bunyut/solar/mineral spend disclosed in the annual report has no separable dollar figure and no material-commitment note [S3 p.151], so it cannot be quantified out. The per-tonne line is nevertheless set at US$4.00/t, not US$4.85/t, because the most recent run-rate is materially lower: 6M26 capex was US$21m against US$32m in 6M25 [S2 p.23], an annualised ~US$42m, so US$4.00/t already sits ABOVE the current run-rate and only below the prior-year average that carried a large deferred-stripping addition. The discretionary expansion projects are not charged separately (capex_other is nil) and are carried at nil symmetrically. Held FLAT in nominal terms thereafter; the most-likely rule holds costs at the last actual in real terms and nothing sources a real rise.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: EXCLUDED from FCFF after the round-1 challenge. The previous build charged the Bunyut port capacity works, the solar pipeline (152 MWp contracted, 86 MWp operating at 2Q26 [S2, F31]) and the new mineral-sector vehicle ITM Mineral Investama [S4] through free cash flow while setting other_revenue to zero and carrying the assets at nil - a one-sided cost. No archived filing discloses segment revenue or a project value for any of them, and the most-likely rule forbids inventing one, so the discretionary expansion spend is removed from the coal DCF and the optionality is carried at nil rather than charged and ignored. Sustaining capex continues to carry the mine's own spend, and the port and solar works that serve the Melak cluster sit inside the operating cost base the LK reports. A sourced revenue or project value would add value; none exists in the record, and the bull adds nothing here for the same reason.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The company pays out a variable share of net profit — its stated policy is to distribute part of each year's profit as cash dividend after allowing for reserves and the development plan [S3]. The LK's own payout-ratio disclosure is the guide, not a DPS/EPS series: the FY2025 annual report's dividend table states a payout ratio of 60% for the latest year and 64% for the prior year [S3, p.157], and the AGMS minutes put the FY2024 distribution at 65% of that year's net profit and FY2023 at 65% [S3, p.171/179] — a 60-65% record. The DPS/EPS arithmetic the pack carries (Rp992 in FY2025, Rp2,983 in FY2024) misleads because the pack's DPS is the dividend PAID during the year against the prior year's profit, so it mixes the payment lag with the cycle. We use the LK's own latest rate, 60% — the last actual, which the base case reproduces — rather than the engine's three-year average of dividends paid over prior-year profit. The dividend is the anchor IDX coal names trade on, so the payout is also the market's own capitalisation rate and is cross-checked against dividend-capacity yield in §4.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: The primary DCF runs to the end of the reserve life with no terminal value, so this scalar only feeds the EV/EBITDA and implied-multiple cross-checks. It is set at zero because a thermal-coal cash-flow stream should not carry perpetual real growth — the coal deck's long-run Newcastle marker is flat in real terms at US$105/t [S0].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: ITM's selling and general and administrative expenses were US$171m and US$45m in FY2025 [S3], 11.5% of net revenue, against US$178m and US$37m in FY2024, 9.3%. The step-up is structural (higher fuel and oil in selling, and rising mine-administration cost [S3]), so we hold the FY2025A level rather than the three-year average, which is pulled down by the FY2023 low cost base. Held flat thereafter in nominal terms.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: The effective rate the LK books, not the 13.5% CCoW headline: royalty expense was US$220.0m on net revenue of US$1,881.1m in FY2025 (11.7%) and US$260.2m on US$2,304.5m in FY2024 (11.3%) [S3, F10]. That blend is the contract rate on the four CCoW/PKP2B mines (IMM Gen I, TCM and JBG Gen II, BEK Gen III) with the far lower IUP schedule on the IUP mines (GPK, TIS, NPR, Kitadin), plus the fact that the resold purchased-coal book carries no royalty — which is why a flat 11.7%, not 13.5%, reproduces what the group actually pays. Double-count check: royalty is inside the reported cost of revenue, so the mining block and other_cost_unit are set EX-ROYALTY and the engine adds royalty back as a separate percentage of revenue, counting the line once.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Fuel is a real and rising cost pressure — the presentation shows diesel at US$0.99/litre in 6M26 against US$0.78 in 6M25 and names rising diesel and global inflation as a cost driver [S2] — but most of ITM's hauling, barging and contract mining is bought at unit rates that already embed the contractor's own diesel, so only a minority of the cost base is directly exposed. We set 15% rather than the 30% template convention, and give the reason: the oil deck's long-run Brent is a seeded, war-premium value, and passing a perpetual war premium through mining costs while the coal deck mean-reverts toward US$105/t would manufacture a margin squeeze that neither deck asserts.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: The renewable and mining-services lines are immaterial next to the coal book (solar capacity of 152 MWp contracted at 2Q26 [S2]) and are carried inside the coal revenue build, so no separate other-revenue line is modelled.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Template constant 10%; the non-coal lines are immaterial to group value.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: ITM is in a net-cash position — cash of US$738m against BORROWINGS of US$18m at 30 June 2026, i.e. net cash of US$720m, with the company reporting net gearing of negative 37% and debt-to-equity of 0.01x [S2, F34, F35] — so no new borrowing is assumed. The data pack's US$804.0m cash / US$99.3m debt is NOT used: its debt line is total debt including roughly US$81m of lease liabilities, and that lease component is a DERIVED residual (the pack's US$99.339m less the company's US$18.0m borrowings), not a disclosed 30 June 2026 figure. The last disclosed lease liability was US$50.153m at 31 December 2025 (US$40.351m current plus US$9.802m non-current [S3 p.142]); the six-month increase is an inference from new vessel, port and mine leases signed since, not a filing figure, and the valuation does not depend on it. Its cash line does not tie to the company's interim disclosure (see section 3). Leases are treated as an operating cost, not as debt: the LK already charges US$36.9m of right-of-use depreciation through selling and G&A expenses [S3, F32], and the US$35.5m of cash lease payments [S3, F33] shows the cost base pays for the leases, so deducting the lease liability from equity as well would count the same obligation twice. The buyback disclosed on 4 November 2026 is funded from internal cash [S7, F41].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: ITM's non-operating line is dominated by finance income on its large net-cash balance, which the engine computes separately via cash_yield; no separate non-operating items are assumed.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: MODELLED ON THE DISCLOSED PROFORMA after the round-2 challenge (C2). The buyback disclosed on 4 November 2026 is sized at up to Rp2.311 trillion over 5 November 2026 to 4 February 2027 [S7, F41], and the company's own proforma puts the count at 1,026m shares from 1,114m after full use of the budget, a 7.9% reduction [S7, F43]. Round 1 carried a zero share change on the argument that a buyback executed above through-cycle value is value-neutral per share; that is wrong, and the challenge is accepted. The per-share arithmetic: US$127.9m of cash (Rp2.311tn at Rp18,075/US$) leaves the company, the count falls 7.9%, and because the purchase price of about Rp26,261 is above the DCF value the cash spent per share retired exceeds the value of each share retired, so value per share FALLS. The engine carries both legs: the cash outflow as a negative bridge item and the count through this input. FY2026E is set at -0.079 and held flat thereafter, so the reduction is taken once rather than compounded. The 20% cap includes the existing 2.4% treasury position [S2], so the effective headroom for new purchases is smaller than the headline; partial execution would leave value per share between the pre-buyback figure and the modelled one.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Engine default carried from history (S0): the three-year average of net working capital over revenue. ITM's working capital is thin and mostly inventory and prepaid taxes, so this is a small drag and is held flat.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history (S0): the three-year average effective rate, close to the Indonesian statutory 22% but lifted by the non-deductible items and the forestry/reclamation charges. Held flat; a different realised price would not move the statutory rate.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history (S0). With borrowings of only US$18m against US$738m of cash at 30 June 2026 [S2, F34, F35] the cost of debt is not a value driver and the default is carried unchanged. The pack's US$99.3m debt line includes lease liabilities and is not used here.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history (S0). ITM holds a large net-cash balance and earns finance income of about US$40m a year on it (S0, S3), consistent with a low-single-digit treasury yield.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history (S0): minority interests take a small share of net profit, consistent with the reported non-controlling interest balance and the 99.99% ownership of the producing subsidiaries [S2].

challenges.answer: Reconciled rather than asserted, and the FY2026E line is now re-based to the run-rate. The 6M26 model-basis EBITDA is US$156m (US$181.2m company basis less the ROU and other D&A the model keeps in the cost lines) on 12.3 Mt at US$12.7/t [S2 p.25, p.21]. The second-half step is now sourced: the guided 3Q26 strip of 10.9x against the H1 10.3x adds about US$1.7/t, so H2 runs near US$11.0/t, and the full year is US$156m plus 14.9 Mt at US$11.0 = about US$320m on 27.2 Mt. The engine now prints US$321.0m (US$11.8/t), not US$293.6m, and other_cost_unit is recalibrated from US$20.7 to US$18.8/t to reconcile to that bridge.

The buyback is now computed, not asserted. The US$127.9m cash outflow (Rp2.311tn at Rp18,075) is a negative item in valuation.bridge and the 7.9% count reduction (1,114m to 1,026m) is an a.share_change input, so the DCF leg is struck on the post-programme count net of the cash and the dividend leg on the higher per-share payout. The net effect is negative because the purchase price is above our value: the DCF leg falls and the dividend leg rises, and section 3 states both directions rather than claiming neutrality. The 20% cap including the existing 2.4% treasury position is noted.

The multiple, the forward yield and the peer anchor are now stated in section 4 rather than left implied, and the leg is described as the most generous of the three. The own-history leg is disclosed as three observations inflated by the 2022-23 supercycle and is no longer called a through-cycle anchor. The multiple itself is computed by the engine as the house blend of peer median and own history and cannot be set by an analyst input without also re-pricing the EV/EBITDA leg, so we disclose the gap rather than silently re-anchor it; the target is left where the house method puts it and the divergence is stated.

An onerous renewal is now a charged state, not only a sentence. The bear carries a 1.8pp add to the booked 11.7% rate, taking the group blend toward the 13.5% CCoW headline on the 7.1 Mt IMM block [S3], and the narrative explains that the extension decision is binary at March 2028 with no source pricing a specific fee. The unmirrored royalty shock is justified in qc_justifications.scenario.mirror: no mechanism lets the booked rate fall, so a negative bull mirror would be an invented benefit. The stale 22.2 Mt is corrected to 22.9 Mt in the bear narrative.

The guided step is now charged. The 3Q26 per-mine guides give 11.68x production-weighted across IMM 14.0x/1.9 Mt, TCM 17.6x/0.8 Mt and BEK 7.7x/2.3 Mt, and about 10.9x once the remaining 0.7 Mt is added [S2 pp.17-18]. FY2026E is the volume-weighted blend of the two halves known (12.3 Mt at the 6M26 actual 10.3x and 14.9 Mt at the guided 10.9x) = 10.6x, and FY2027E onward holds the guided 10.9x without compounding. The costs of the step are charged in the model, which is why the FY2026E cost base rises rather than falls.

Both defects fixed. The reverse-DCF label now reads the FY2027E deck marker, which is the marker the factor is measured against. The 6M26 ASP of US$81.0/t in qc_justifications.drift.realisation is cited to S2 p.21, with F16 retained only as the 2Q26 print it actually is.

The wording is corrected and the divergence stated: on ITM own five-year average EV/EBITDA multiple the leg would still sit roughly a third above the DCF, not a little above it. The number is described relatively because prose carries no typed figures.

The unsourced superlatives are downgraded. Section 1 now says the unit cost sits inside the band the peer COAL names book rather than in the first part of a global cost curve we cannot source, and section 2 drops the first-quartile claim for the same reason. Section 6 no longer claims a position above the sector median: it says the group reports third-party scores but names neither score nor verifiable median, and describes only what is disclosed.

The prose now describes the run the engine makes. The investment summary, section 1 and all three section-4 paragraphs that carried the claim now describe a full-life DCF carried to reserve depletion with no terminal value (life_end FY2041E), and the tail statement is corrected to the engine's sign: free cash flow is thin in FY2033E and negative from FY2034E to FY2039E at deck prices, but the FY2040E working-capital release and the small FY2041E tail more than offset those years, so the tail ADDS under one per cent to the NAV (pv_sum 314.22 against cum_pv at FY2032E of 311.70) and the model carries it. The FY2032E-cut claim is gone from every instance, including the thesis bullet the challenge did not list. No model input changed, so val.methods.dcf_life.value is the same full-life value it always was.

flags.message: FY+1 priced at FY2025A benchmark and volume gives EBITDA 62.5 vs the actual 293.5 (-79%): reconcile costs, royalty or realisation with the filing, or justify the change
flags.justification: The model's FY2025A EBITDA of US$293.5m is reconciled to the LK-reported US$343.1m, not asserted against a model-derived actual. The company computes EBITDA as operating income of US$266.975m plus total D&A of US$76.166m [S5 p.23]; this model computes it as the same operating income plus only the US$26.862m of property, plant and equipment depreciation charged to cost of revenue [S3, F8]. The US$49.6m difference is the company's D&A add-back that the model deliberately does not make: ROU depreciation of US$36.945m [S3, F32] plus about US$12.4m of other depreciation/amortisation carried in the cost lines. Leases are treated as an operating cost, not as debt, because the cost base already charges the ROU depreciation and the US$35.493m of cash lease payments [S3, F33] matches it; adding the ROU charge back to EBITDA while keeping the lease liability in net debt would count the same obligation twice. Separately, and cross-referencing the drift.realisation flag, the gate re-prices FY2025A at the realisation set on the 6M26 actual, comparing the FY2026E ratio of 0.614 with a FY2025A cost base at the 0.7167 ratio: that gap is the forecast-year realisation difference (67% of FY26 sales are fixed-price and only 24% indexed [S2, F26]) plus the sourced strip step from 9.4x [S3, F7] to the 10.6-10.9x path that blends the 6M26 actual with the 3Q26 guides [S2, F18], not a mis-specified history.

flags.message: a.realisation moves +17% from FY2026E to FY2045E: source the change or hold it

The move is one step at the year the contracts roll, not a year-on-year creep, and it is the same ratio the last two completed fiscal years actually printed.

flags.message: bear and bull shock different drivers (bear only ['a.royalty_rate'], bull only [])
flags.justification: The ONLY unmirrored shock is a.royalty_rate, and the asymmetry is sourced rather than cautious: the bear carries a 1.8pp add to the booked rate if the IMM CCoW Gen I is renewed on onerous terms, taking the group blend from the 11.7% the LK books toward the 13.5% CCoW contract headline [S3, F10]. There is no mechanism in the record that lets the booked royalty rate fall below what the contract and the government schedule set, so a negative mirror would be an invented benefit; the bull therefore earns its return from price and the top of the guided volume range instead. Every other driver (d.coal.newc, a.volume, a.capped_share) is mirrored exactly. The base carries the booked 11.7% rate throughout [S3, F10].

flags.message: a.volume: bear 0.78 vs bull 1.01 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: The bear's 0.78 volume clip is sized to Indominco Mandiri, not a generic quota: IMM is 7.1 Mt of the 22.0-22.9 Mt FY26 production plan (22.9 Mt at the top of the range) [S2, F27, F28], holds 31 Mt of reserves and its CCoW Gen I expires in March 2028 [S2, F29], so a failed extension removes about three-tenths of mined volume from that year; the engine shocks the whole forecast, so 0.78 is the PV-equivalent loss. The bull's 1.01x is the TOP of the company's own 26.9-27.5 Mt sales target (27.5 / 27.2 Mt) [S2, F15, F28], not a mirror of the bear, because no archived source quantifies Bunyut throughput or an NPR uplift and RKAB approval plus approved capacity cap output [S2]. The asymmetry is sourced, not cautious: the benchmark, the capped-share and the realised-price shocks are mirrored exactly, and the bull earns its return from price rather than invented volume.

flags.message: PKP2B royalty is contract-specific: set a.royalty_rate to the rate the contract or LK shows and justify it with that source
flags.justification: a.royalty_rate is the LK's own effective rate, not the CCoW headline: royalty expense was US$220.0m on net revenue of US$1,881.1m in FY2025, i.e. 11.7% [S3, F10], and US$260.2m on US$2,304.5m in FY2024, i.e. 11.3% [S3]. That blend is the contract rate on ITM's four CCoW/PKP2B mines (IMM Gen I, TCM Gen II, BEK Gen III, JBG Gen II) over the far lower IUP schedule on its IUP mines (GPK, TIS, NPR, Kitadin) [S3], which is why a flat 11.7% — not the 13.5% CCoW rate — reproduces what the group actually books. ITM is a PKP2B holder for royalty purposes, so the contract rate, not the IUPK step table, is the applicable schedule.

flags.message: balance-sheet debt restated at 0.18x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The pack's 30 June 2026 debt line of US$99.339m is total debt INCLUDING lease liabilities, not borrowings. The company's own balance sheet at the same date shows borrowings of US$18m [S2, F35], and the difference of about US$81m is the lease liability — a DERIVED residual (US$99.339m less US$18.0m), not a disclosed 30 June 2026 figure. The last disclosed lease liability was US$50.153m at 31 December 2025 (US$40.351m current plus US$9.802m non-current [S3 p.142]); the six-month increase is an inference from new vessel, port and mine leases signed since, not a filing figure, and no valuation input depends on it. We restate the bridge to the US$18m borrowing line because the DCF already pays for the leases through the cost base: ROU depreciation of US$36.9m [S3, F32] is charged in selling and G&A, matched by US$35.5m of cash lease payments [S3, F33]. Deducting the lease liability from equity as well would double-count the obligation. The cash line is restated to the company's US$738m for the same reason [S2, F34]; the pack's US$804.0m does not tie to the interim disclosure.
